title: Largest Genetic Study of Fibromyalgia Confirms It Is a Nervous System Disorder, Not Autoimmune
excerpt: An international team analysed DNA from 2.5 million people, identified 26 risk genes concentrated in the brain and nerves, and found a surprising link to the gene behind Huntington's disease.
body:
• A genome-wide study of 2.5 million adults identified 26 genetic risk loci for fibromyalgia — the first robust genetic map of the condition.
  • The implicated genes are concentrated in brain and nerve tissue, providing the strongest evidence yet that fibromyalgia is a central nervous system disorder rather than an autoimmune disease.
  • The strongest genetic association was with a variant in HTT, the same gene responsible for Huntington's disease, opening a potential drug-repurposing pathway.
  • Despite being diagnosed three times more often in women, the genetic architecture of fibromyalgia was nearly identical between sexes, suggesting non-genetic factors drive the prevalence gap.

Decades of Dismissal, Now Genetic Proof

For millions of people living with fibromyalgia — a condition marked by chronic widespread pain, fatigue, and cognitive difficulties — validation has been hard to come by. Doctors have questioned its existence. Patients have been told the pain is psychological. A landmark study published in Nature Medicine may finally change that.

An international team of 53 researchers across seven countries analysed genetic data from more than 2.5 million adults, including roughly 55,000 fibromyalgia patients. They identified DNA variants in 26 regions of the genome that increase the risk of developing the condition — the first comprehensive genetic map of fibromyalgia ever produced.

The genes flagged by the study are overwhelmingly active in brain and nerve cells, not in immune tissue. That finding delivers what the researchers call "robust genetic validation" that fibromyalgia is primarily a disorder of the central nervous system, not an autoimmune condition as has long been debated.

"This work changes how we think about fibromyalgia at a fundamental level. For decades, patients have been dismissed or told their pain is simply psychological. Our findings confirm the condition has a clear biological basis."

— Dr. Michael Wainberg, Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute, University of Toronto

A Surprising Link to Huntington's Disease

Among the 26 genetic variants identified, the strongest association was with a coding variant in the HTT gene — the same gene whose mutations cause Huntington's disease, a severe and fatal neurodegenerative disorder.

Another variant pointed to GPR52, a receptor that regulates HTT levels and is already being investigated as a drug target for Huntington's. The connection raises an intriguing possibility: therapies under development for Huntington's could potentially be repurposed for fibromyalgia.

A second therapeutic target emerged in CELF4, a gene already under investigation for chronic pain gene therapies. Other implicated genes — including CAMKV, DCC, DRD2/NCAM1, and MDGA2 — play diverse roles in neural signalling and brain development.

Not Autoimmune, but Complex

The autoimmune question has lingered over fibromyalgia for years. The study found no significant genetic signal in the MHC region — the part of the genome most associated with autoimmune diseases — and no enrichment of fibromyalgia heritability in immune cell types.

However, the researchers noted weak genetic correlations with autoimmune disorders including Sjögren's syndrome and rheumatoid arthritis, and five of the discovered loci showed associations with white blood cell count. The picture that emerges is of a condition rooted in the nervous system that may have an immune component, rather than one driven by autoimmunity.

The study also revealed strong genetic overlap between fibromyalgia and other chronic pain conditions — low back pain, irritable bowel syndrome, and post-traumatic stress disorder all shared genetic correlations above 0.7 with fibromyalgia.

"We know that chronic pain syndromes cluster together in individuals and families and are genetically similar. Targeting the shared mechanisms underlying them could potentially benefit a whole cluster of disorders."

— Dr. Frances Williams, King's College London

The Gender Paradox

Fibromyalgia is diagnosed roughly three times more often in women than in men. But the study found the genetic architecture of the condition was nearly identical between sexes — suggesting the prevalence gap is driven by non-genetic factors such as hormonal influences, environmental exposures, or differences in how pain is reported and diagnosed.

What This Means for Patients

The findings do not yet provide a genetic test for diagnosing fibromyalgia or a new treatment. But they offer concrete molecular starting points that could guide future research into better diagnosis and targeted therapies.

The study was jointly led by Dr. Wainberg at the University of Toronto, Dr. Nasa Sinnott-Armstrong at the Fred Hutch Cancer Center and University of Washington, and Dr. Hanna Ollila at the University of Helsinki and Massachusetts General Hospital. The data drew from 11 cohorts across the US, UK, Finland, Estonia, Denmark, and Iceland.

The researchers have since founded the Chronic Pain Genomics Consortium to apply the same approach to other pain syndromes, starting with pelvic pain. For the estimated 2% of the global population living with fibromyalgia, the message is clear: the pain is real, it is biological, and science is finally catching up.
